title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 6
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Full practice tests
summary: A full, timed Reading and Writing section in Digital SAT format: two 32-minute modules of 27 questions each, with a reason for every answer choice, your score by skill and links back to the lessons.

blocks.text: This is a complete Reading and Writing section in the format of the Digital SAT: **two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each (54 questions, 64 minutes)**. Every question has one short passage (or a pair of short passages) and four choices. Inside each module the questions come in the usual order: Craft and Structure, then Information and Ideas, then Standard English Conventions, and Expression of Ideas last. All passages and questions were written for this course.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone and about 70 minutes free. Do the whole test in one sitting.
The timer starts when you begin a module. Aim for about 1 minute 11 seconds per question, and do not spend more than 2 minutes on any single question.

Inside a module you can move back and forth between questions. When the 32 minutes end, the module closes. In the real test, you cannot go back to Module 1 once Module 2 starts, so treat this test the same way.
There is no penalty for wrong answers. Never leave a question blank: if time is short, eliminate what you can and guess.
At the end you will see your number correct, your result for each module and each skill, a reason for every answer choice, and links to the lessons for your weakest skills.

blocks.title: About your result
blocks.text: The score shown at the end is a practice percentage (the number of questions you answered correctly). It is not an official SAT score. Official Reading and Writing scores are reported on a scale of 200–800, and this page does not convert your result to that scale.

blocks.title: قبل ما تبدأ
blocks.text: اقعد في مكان هادي من غير موبايل، وخلّي معاك حوالي ساعة وربع. الامتحان موديولين، كل واحد 27 سؤال في 32 دقيقة، يعني تقريبًا دقيقة وعشر ثواني للسؤال. جوه الموديول تقدر ترجع لأي سؤال، لكن لما الوقت يخلص الموديول بيقفل، وفي الامتحان الحقيقي مفيش رجوع لـ Module 1. مفيش خصم على الإجابة الغلط، فمتسيبش ولا سؤال فاضي. في الآخر هتلاقي سبب لكل اختيار ليه صح أو غلط، ولينكات للدروس اللي محتاج تراجعها. والنسبة اللي هتظهر للتدريب بس، مش درجة SAT رسمية.

blocks.title: Digital SAT Reading and Writing — Practice Test 6
blocks.intro: Two modules, 27 questions each, 32 minutes per module. In the real test, 2 questions in each module are unscored pretest questions, and Module 2 adapts to how well you did in Module 1 (it becomes harder or easier). Here all 54 questions count: Module 1 is a mixed-difficulty module, and Module 2 is the harder version. Questions follow the usual order: Craft and Structure, Information and Ideas, Standard English Conventions, then Expression of Ideas. Once Module 1 ends, you cannot go back to it. Answer every question — there is no penalty for guessing.

questions.p: Psychologist Hana Mertz found that toddlers who watched an adult struggle with a task before succeeding kept trying longer on their own puzzles than toddlers who watched an adult succeed easily. The finding suggests that even very young children ______ lessons about effort from the behavior of the adults around them.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The toddlers changed their own behavior after watching an adult, so they learned, or "drew," a lesson from what they saw. "Discard" reverses this, since the children clearly used what they saw; "invent" ignores that the lesson came from the adult.
ce: Opposite meaning: the toddlers' longer effort shows they kept the lesson, not threw it away.
The lesson came from watching the adult, so the children did not make it up themselves.
Nothing in the text is about hiding anything; the children's behavior openly showed the lesson.
Correct: to "draw lessons from" something means to learn from it, and the toddlers learned about effort just by watching.

questions.p: Built in the 1960s and 1970s from rough, unpainted concrete, many Brutalist buildings were admired by architects for their honesty about materials. To many members of the public, however, the same bare walls seemed ______, and several of these buildings were later demolished after years of complaints that they looked cold and unwelcoming.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The public complained that the buildings looked "cold and unwelcoming," which is what "forbidding" means. "Ornate" fails because the walls are described as bare, and "festive" is the opposite of cold.
ce: "Ornate" means heavily decorated, the opposite of bare concrete walls.
Correct: "forbidding" means unfriendly and threatening, matching "cold and unwelcoming".
Nothing suggests the walls looked weak; the complaints were that they looked cold.
"Festive" means cheerful, which contradicts "cold and unwelcoming".

questions.p: Unlike most fish, the African lungfish can breathe air. When its pond dries up, it burrows into the mud and wraps itself in a cocoon of hardened mucus. Inside the cocoon, with its body processes slowed almost to a stop, the fish can remain ______ for months until the rains return.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: With its body processes almost stopped, the fish is alive but inactive, so "dormant" fits. "Agitated" is the opposite, and "exposed" contradicts the detail that the fish is buried and wrapped in a cocoon.
ce: Correct: "dormant" means alive but inactive, exactly what the cocoon stage describes.
An agitated animal is restless and active, the opposite of a body "slowed almost to a stop".
The fish is buried in mud and wrapped in a cocoon, so it is protected, not exposed.
A migratory animal travels long distances; this fish stays in one place under the mud.

questions.p: When the Metropolitan Railway opened in London in 1863, it became the world's first underground railway. Its steam locomotives filled the tunnels with smoke, yet the public was not ______: tens of thousands of passengers rode the line on its very first day.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: "Yet" signals that the smoke did not stop people, and the crowds prove it, so the public was not "deterred." "Transported" fails because the passengers were in fact carried by the trains.
ce: The public was transported in large numbers, so saying it was "not transported" contradicts the text.
The text is about whether smoke kept people away, not about whether they knew about the line.
Whether people had jobs on the railway has nothing to do with the smoke or the crowds.
Correct: despite the smoke, people were not put off, as the huge first-day crowds show.

questions.p: In many classrooms of the early 1900s, rows of heavy desks faced the teacher, and children were expected to sit still and listen. In 1907, physician Maria Montessori opened a school for young children in Rome that broke with this model. Its furniture was child-sized and light enough for the children to move, and learning materials were placed on low shelves where children could choose them for themselves. Montessori believed that children learn best when they are free to direct their own activity.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It describes a common classroom arrangement, presents a school that departed from it, and then states the belief behind that change.
It presents a theory of learning and then describes research that disproved it.
It compares two schools in Rome and argues that one was more successful.
It describes a problem with child-sized furniture and then proposes a solution.
questions.e: The text moves from the usual classroom, to Montessori's different school, to the belief behind it. The "theory disproved" choice reverses the ending, which supports Montessori's idea rather than rejecting it.
ce: Correct: rows of desks (common model) → Montessori's school (departure) → her belief about self-directed learning.
No research disproves anything; the text ends by stating Montessori's belief, not rejecting it.
Only one school is described, and the text never judges success.
Child-sized furniture is part of the new approach, not a problem to be solved.

questions.p: Painter Layla Haddad's early canvases were crowded with detail: every leaf, brick, and fold of cloth was carefully rendered. __In her final decade, however, she began leaving large areas of canvas almost bare, suggesting a whole street with only a few strokes of gray.__ Critics who had admired her precision were at first puzzled, but many now consider these spare late works her finest.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It explains why critics preferred Haddad's early works to her later ones.
It offers an example of the detail that characterized Haddad's early canvases.
It describes the technique Haddad used to paint leaves and bricks.
It introduces a change in Haddad's style that contrasts with the approach described in the previous sentence.
questions.e: The underlined sentence, signaled by "however," presents a new, spare style that contrasts with the detailed early work. It does not illustrate the early detail, and it does not explain critics' preferences.
ce: The text says many critics now consider the late works her finest, and the underlined sentence gives no reasons.
The underlined sentence describes bare canvas, the opposite of the detailed early style.
Leaves and bricks belong to the early detailed paintings; the underlined sentence is about the later, spare ones.
Correct: "however" marks the shift from crowded detail to nearly bare canvases.

questions.p:
Text 1
For decades, many teacher-training courses taught that each student has a preferred "learning style"—visual, auditory, or hands-on—and that students learn more when lessons are presented in that style. Teacher trainer Mariam Lotfi still recommends that teachers test students' styles at the start of each year and plan lessons to match.

Text 2
A team led by educational psychologist Tarek Nassar asked students which style they preferred and then taught each student either in that style or in a different one. Nearly all students reported a clear preference. On a test a week later, however, students taught in their preferred style scored no higher than students taught in another style.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Nassar's team (Text 2) most likely respond to Lotfi's recommendation (Text 1)?
c: By agreeing with it, since nearly all the students in their study reported a clear preference
By arguing that auditory lessons are more effective than visual lessons for all students
By claiming that students do not have any preferences about how they learn
By questioning it, since their results suggest that matching lessons to students' preferred styles does not improve learning
questions.e: Nassar's team found no score benefit from matching lessons to preferred styles, so they would doubt the value of Lotfi's plan. The "agreeing" choice confuses having a preference with learning better because of it.
ce: Having a preference is not the same as learning better with it; the test scores showed no benefit.
The study does not compare styles with each other; it finds that matching made no difference.
Text 2 says nearly all students did report a clear preference.
Correct: students taught in their preferred style scored no higher, which undercuts the reason for matching.

questions.p: Biologists once assumed that a honeybee colony fought disease only through the immune systems of individual bees. Research has shown that colonies also defend themselves as a group. Worker bees coat the inside of the hive with propolis, a sticky resin collected from trees that slows the growth of bacteria and fungi, and some colonies gather more of it when they are infected. Other workers detect sick or dead young bees and remove them before an infection can spread.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Propolis is the most effective defense that honeybees have against disease.
Honeybee colonies protect themselves from disease through group behaviors as well as through the immune systems of individual bees.
Honeybees' individual immune systems are weaker than those of most other insects.
Worker bees collect resin from trees mainly to strengthen the walls of the hive.
questions.e: The text sets up an old belief (individual immunity only) and then shows two collective defenses, so the main idea is that colonies also defend themselves as a group. The propolis choice picks one detail and overstates it.
ce: Too narrow and too strong: propolis is one example, and the text never ranks defenses.
Correct: the text corrects an old assumption by showing two group defenses.
The text makes no comparison with other insects.
The text says the resin slows the growth of bacteria and fungi, not that it strengthens walls.

questions.p: In 1920, economist Talaat Harb founded Banque Misr, a bank owned and run by Egyptians at a time when most of the country's banks were controlled by foreign investors. Harb used the bank's capital to establish Egyptian companies in fields such as textiles, air travel, and cinema. Studio Misr, set up by the bank in 1935, became one of the most important film studios in the Arab world.
questions.q: According to the text, what was unusual about Banque Misr when it was founded?
c: It was owned and run by Egyptians, unlike most banks in the country at that time.
It was the first bank to lend money to film studios outside Egypt.
It was controlled by foreign investors who wanted to build textile factories.
It was founded in the same year as Studio Misr.
questions.e: The text says the bank was Egyptian-owned when most banks were foreign-controlled. The "foreign investors" choice reverses this detail, and the dates show the bank and studio were founded fifteen years apart.
ce: Correct: the text contrasts it with banks "controlled by foreign investors".
The text mentions only Studio Misr, which the bank itself set up in Egypt.
Reversed: the foreign-controlled banks were the other banks, not Banque Misr.
The bank dates from 1920 and the studio from 1935.

questions.p: Psychologist Nadia Saber hypothesizes that people judge a task as easier to perform when its instructions are printed in a clear, simple typeface than when the same instructions are printed in a typeface that is hard to read.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Saber's hypothesis?
c: Participants read text in clear typefaces faster than text in hard-to-read typefaces.
Participants said that clear typefaces looked more attractive than hard-to-read ones.

Participants who read exercise instructions in a clear typeface estimated that the routine would take less time and effort than participants who read identical instructions in a hard-to-read typeface.
Participants who received longer instructions judged a task as harder than those who received shorter instructions, regardless of typeface.
questions.e: Only the exercise finding keeps the instructions the same, changes just the typeface, and measures how hard the task seems, exactly as the hypothesis predicts. Faster reading is the tempting trap, but it says nothing about judgments of the task.
ce: Reading speed is not the same as judging how hard the task itself will be.
Attractiveness is not the claim; the hypothesis is about how difficult the task seems.
Correct: same instructions, different typeface, and the clear typeface made the task seem easier.
This is about length, not typeface, and "regardless of typeface" gives no support.

questions.p: In an original letter written in the style of the nineteenth century, a young architect describes his first visit to a newly built covered market in the capital. In the letter, he suggests that the building impressed him more through its engineering than through its decoration.
questions.q: Which quotation from the letter most effectively illustrates this claim?
c: "The carved figures above the entrance are the finest I have seen in any city, and I stood a full quarter hour admiring them."
"The stone figures over the doors hardly held my eye; it was the great iron roof, spanning the whole hall without a single pillar, that left me speechless."
"The crowds of buyers pressing between the stalls made it difficult to stop and look about me as I had hoped."
"I had read of this market in my father's newspapers long before I ever thought to see it for myself."
questions.e: The claim compares engineering with decoration, and only the quotation about the iron roof does both: it brushes aside the stone figures and praises the pillar-free roof. The "carved figures" quotation reverses the claim.
ce: This praises the decoration, the opposite of the claim.
Correct: it dismisses the decoration and is amazed by the structure.
This describes the crowds, not a comparison of engineering and decoration.
This is background about the writer, not his reaction to the building.

questions.p:
Average reading score of sixth-grade students, by minutes of independent reading per week
Minutes per week | Average score (out of 100)
0–30 | 58
31–60 | 64
61–120 | 71
More than 120 | 73

A district researcher concluded that students who read independently for more time each week tended to have higher reading scores, although the gain became smaller at the highest level of reading time. ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's conclusion?
c: Students who read for 31–60 minutes per week had an average score of 64.
Students who read for more than 120 minutes per week had the highest average score, 73.
Average scores fell from 73 to 58 as reading time increased.
Average scores rose from 58 for students who read 0–30 minutes per week to 71 for those who read 61–120 minutes, but rose only to 73 for those who read more than 120 minutes.
questions.e: The conclusion has two parts, a rising trend and a smaller gain at the top, and only one choice shows both (58 → 71, then only to 73). The "highest score" choice is accurate but supports only the first part.
ce: One figure alone cannot show a rising trend or a smaller gain at the top.
This shows the top group but not that the gain became smaller.
Reversed: scores rose as reading time increased.
Correct: it shows the rise and the smaller final gain, the two parts of the conclusion.

questions.p:
Germination rates of seeds from a tropical tree, by treatment
Seed treatment | Seeds that germinated (%)
Taken directly from fruit | 12
Collected from bird droppings | 47
Scratched with sandpaper | 44

Ecologist Samir Farouk suspects that the seeds of a tropical tree germinate better after passing through a bird's gut mainly because the seed coat gets scratched on the way, not because of any chemical in the bird's gut. To test this idea, he compared three groups of seeds. ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Farouk's suspicion?
c: Seeds collected from bird droppings had the highest germination rate, 47%.
Only 12% of seeds taken directly from fruit germinated.
Seeds from bird droppings germinated at about four times the rate of seeds taken directly from fruit.
Seeds scratched with sandpaper germinated at a rate of 44%, close to the 47% rate for seeds from bird droppings and far above the 12% rate for seeds taken directly from fruit.
questions.e: To show that scratching is the main cause, the data must show that sandpaper alone gives nearly the same rate as a trip through a bird (44% vs 47%). The "four times" choice is true but cannot tell scratching apart from chemicals.
ce: This shows birds help, but not whether scratching alone explains it.
This gives the baseline only, with no comparison to scratched seeds.
True, but it does not separate scratching from gut chemicals.
Correct: scratching alone, with no bird chemicals, produced nearly the same benefit.

questions.p: In the 1850s, most physicians believed that cholera spread through foul air. During an outbreak in London in 1854, physician John Snow found that many of the victims had drawn their water from a single public pump on Broad Street. Yet very few workers at a brewery on that street fell ill, even though they breathed the same air as their neighbors. The brewery had its own well, and its workers rarely drank water from the pump. These observations suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the disease was spread through water from the pump rather than through the air of the neighborhood.
drinking beer was what protected the brewery workers from cholera.
the brewery workers were healthier than their neighbors before the outbreak began.
cholera was carried into the neighborhood by people arriving from outside London.
questions.e: The workers shared the neighborhood's air but not its pump water, and they stayed healthy, which points to the water as the cause. The beer choice is the trap: the text never mentions beer and highlights the separate well instead.
ce: Correct: same air but different water led to different results, pointing to the water.
The text never says what the workers drank instead; what it stresses is that they avoided the pump's water and had their own well.
Nothing in the text describes the workers' earlier health.
The text never mentions travelers or where the disease came from.

questions.p: In 1937, Pablo Picasso painted Guernica in response to the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil ______ enormous black, white, and gray canvas is more than seven meters wide.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Both parts are complete sentences, so they must be separated, here with a period. A comma alone creates a comma splice, and no punctuation creates a run-on.
ce: Comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two complete sentences.
Run-on: two complete sentences are fused with no punctuation.
Correct: a period correctly separates two complete sentences.
"That" turns the second sentence into a clause that does not fit grammatically.

questions.p: The axolotl—a salamander found in the wild only in a few lakes and canals near Mexico ______ can regrow lost limbs, parts of its heart, and even sections of its spinal cord.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The phrase describing the axolotl begins with a dash, so it must end with a dash before the main verb "can regrow." A comma does not match the opening dash.
ce: Correct: the second dash closes the extra information opened by the first dash.
Mismatched pair: extra information opened with a dash must close with a dash, not a comma.
A semicolon would split the subject "The axolotl" from its verb "can regrow".
Without a closing dash, the extra information runs straight into the verb.

questions.p: Before the 1840s, surgeons faced a grim ______ there was no reliable way to keep patients unconscious during an operation. The first widely reported public demonstration of ether anesthesia took place in Boston in 1846.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "Surgeons faced a grim limitation" is a complete sentence, and what follows explains it, so a colon fits. A comma alone joins two complete sentences and creates a comma splice.
ce: Comma splice: "there was no reliable way…" is a complete sentence.
Run-on: the two complete sentences are fused with no punctuation.
"Which there was no reliable way…" is not grammatical.
Correct: a colon after a complete sentence introduces the explanation of what the limitation was.

questions.p: The guided tour of the city's modernist buildings included the central library, completed in 1958; the train station, with its curved concrete ______ and the old post office, now a museum.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Each item in this list contains its own comma, so the items are separated by semicolons, and the first separator is already a semicolon. A comma here breaks the pattern and blurs where items end.
ce: The list already uses a semicolon between items; switching to a comma makes the list unclear.
A colon cannot separate two items in a list.
With no punctuation, the second and third items run together.
Correct: items that contain commas are separated by semicolons (SAT/ACT extra rule), matching the first semicolon.

questions.p: In a study by psychologist Ahmed Zaki, volunteers who described a stressful memory aloud to a calm ______ lower heart rates afterward than volunteers who described the same memory to no one.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The subject is "volunteers who described a stressful memory aloud to a calm listener," and its verb is "had," so no punctuation may come between them. The comma is the tempting trap because the subject is long.
ce: A single comma cannot separate a subject from its verb.
A single dash cannot separate a subject from its verb.
A semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and "had lower heart rates" has no subject.
Correct: no punctuation belongs between the long subject and its verb "had".

questions.p: The collection of letters written by nurses who served in field hospitals during the First World War ______ a vivid picture of daily life in wartime medicine.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The subject is "collection," not "letters," "nurses" or "hospitals," so the verb must be singular: "offers." The other choices agree with the nearest plural nouns.
ce: Plural verb, but the subject "collection" is singular.
Plural verb; it agrees with "letters" or "nurses", not with the real subject.
Correct: the singular subject "collection" needs the singular verb "offers".
Plural verb, so it does not agree with the singular subject "collection".

questions.p: Hoping to make art available to ordinary citizens, the Mexican government in the 1920s ______ painters such as Diego Rivera to cover the walls of public buildings with murals.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The sentence needs a main verb for "the Mexican government," and only "commissioned" is finite. "Commissioning," "to commission" and "having commissioned" all leave the sentence without a main verb.
ce: An -ing form cannot be the main verb of a sentence, so the sentence would have no main verb.
An infinitive cannot be the main verb, so the sentence would be a fragment.
Correct: the subject "the Mexican government" needs a finite, past-tense verb.
A participle phrase cannot be the main verb; the sentence would be incomplete.

questions.p: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images of DNA, including the famous Photo 51, were essential to the discovery of this ______ double-helix structure in 1953.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "This" points to one molecule, DNA, and the double-helix structure belongs to it, so the singular possessive "molecule's" is needed. "Molecules'" wrongly makes it plural, which does not fit "this."
ce: Correct: singular possessive — the structure of this one molecule, DNA.
This is a plural with no possession, and "this" cannot come before a plural noun.
Plural possessive, but "this" points to one molecule, DNA.
Without an apostrophe, nothing shows that the structure belongs to the molecule.

questions.p: For much of the twentieth century, left-handed children in many schools were made to write with their right hands. Many teachers of the time believed that switching hands would help these children fit in. ______ the practice often caused frustration and slowed the children's progress in writing.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: The teachers expected the practice to help, but it actually caused frustration, so "In reality" sets the real outcome against the belief. "Therefore" wrongly treats the bad result as a consequence of the hope.
ce: The result is not similar to the teachers' belief; it goes against it.
Correct: it contrasts what teachers believed with what actually happened.
The frustration was not a result of the teachers' hopes; it contradicts them.
Frustration is not an example of the teachers' belief.

questions.p: A sea star that loses an arm can usually grow a replacement over several months. ______ in a few species, a single arm that breaks away can regrow an entire body, producing a complete new animal.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: The second sentence describes a more remarkable version of the same ability, so "Even more strikingly" fits. "In other words" fails because the sentence adds new information instead of restating.
ce: Regrowing a whole body is not caused by regrowing an arm.
Nothing in the first sentence makes the second surprising in a contrasting way.
Correct: growing a whole animal from one arm goes further than regrowing one arm.
The second sentence adds a more extreme ability; it does not restate the first.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Sydney Opera House is a performing arts center in Sydney, Australia.
• It was designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon.
• Utzon's design was chosen in an international competition in 1957.
• Its roof is made of a series of white, shell-like concrete sections.
• The building opened in 1973.
questions.q: The student wants to introduce the Sydney Opera House to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Jørn Utzon was a Danish architect.
Utzon's design was chosen in 1957, and the building opened in 1973.
Its roof is made of a series of white, shell-like concrete sections.
The Sydney Opera House, a performing arts center in Australia known for its white, shell-like concrete roof, was designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon and opened in 1973.
questions.e: An introduction for a new audience must say what the building is and give key facts, and only one choice does. The "1957 and 1973" choice gives dates but never says what the Sydney Opera House is.
ce: This is about Utzon only and does not introduce the building.
It assumes the reader already knows what building and design are meant.
"Its" has no clear reference for a new reader, and the sentence gives no basic identification.
Correct: it says what and where the building is, what it looks like, who designed it and when it opened.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Before the 1920s, a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes was usually fatal.
• In 1921, researchers at the University of Toronto, including Frederick Banting and Charles Best, isolated insulin.
• In January 1922, a 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson became the first person to receive an insulin injection to treat diabetes.
• Insulin is still used to treat diabetes today.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize the importance of the 1921 discovery. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best worked at the University of Toronto.
The isolation of insulin in 1921 turned type 1 diabetes from a disease that was usually fatal into one that could be treated, and insulin is still used to treat diabetes today.
Leonard Thompson was 14 years old when he received an insulin injection in January 1922.
Type 1 diabetes was usually fatal before the 1920s.
questions.e: To show importance, the sentence must connect the discovery to its effect: a usually fatal disease became treatable, and insulin is still used. The "usually fatal" choice states the problem but never mentions the discovery.
ce: This gives names and a place but no sense of why the discovery mattered.
Correct: it shows the change the discovery made and its lasting use.
A detail about one patient, without showing the wider importance.
This gives the background but does not connect it to the discovery.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Educational researcher Mona Selim compared two ways of teaching fractions to fourth graders.
• Group 1 learned with blocks they could move and combine.
• Group 2 learned from drawings in a textbook.
• After four weeks, both groups scored similarly on a test of basic fraction problems.
• Group 1 scored higher on problems that asked students to explain their reasoning.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize where the two groups' results differed. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: After four weeks, both groups scored similarly on a test of basic fraction problems.
Selim compared two ways of teaching fractions to fourth graders.

Although both groups did similarly on basic fraction problems, students who learned with blocks outscored those who learned from textbook drawings on problems that asked them to explain their reasoning.
One group of fourth graders learned fractions with blocks they could move and combine.
questions.e: Only one choice names the area where the groups' results differed: explaining reasoning. The "scored similarly" choice reports a result, but it is the similarity, the opposite of the goal.
ce: This shows where the results were the same, not where they differed.
This describes the study but gives no results.
Correct: it pinpoints the one area where the groups differed.
This describes one group's method, with no result or comparison.

questions.p: Early researchers of child development often described young infants as passive, simply ______ whatever sights and sounds reached them. Later experiments, which measured how long babies stared at surprising events, revealed that infants actively form expectations about how objects should behave.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The blank describes the old "passive" view, so it needs a word for simply taking things in: "absorbing." "Anticipating" describes the later finding that infants form expectations, so it reverses the contrast.
ce: Anticipating is active, but the early view described infants as passive; active expectations are the later finding.
To interrogate is to question actively, which contradicts "passive".
Correct: passively taking in whatever reaches them is what "absorbing" means here.
Dismissing is an active judgment, and the early view did not say infants rejected anything.

questions.p: Critics often treat the paintings of Omar Badran as purely decorative, but such a reading is ______: his bright geometric patterns are copied from the tiles of buildings that were demolished as his city modernized, and many viewers who remember those buildings find the paintings deeply mournful.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The text says the "purely decorative" reading leaves out the paintings' meaning of loss, so it is oversimplified, or "reductive." "Exhaustive" is the opposite of what the text claims.
ce: Exhaustive means complete and thorough, the opposite of a reading that misses the paintings' meaning.
Correct: calling the paintings "purely decorative" reduces them and ignores their deeper meaning.
The text argues against this reading, so it is not presented as convincing.
Redundant means repeated or unnecessary, which is not the problem the text describes.

questions.p: Once found only in the homes of the wealthy, the electric refrigerator had become ______ in one country's kitchens within a few decades: a national household survey there found that more than nine out of ten homes owned one.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: The colon explains the blank: more than nine out of ten homes owned a refrigerator, so it had become "ubiquitous," or found almost everywhere. "Conspicuous" is the tempting trap, but it means noticeable, not widespread, and "obsolete" reverses the point.
ce: Obsolete means out of use, but nine out of ten homes still owned one.
Conspicuous means standing out, but something found in almost every home no longer stands out; the text is about how widespread it was.
Correct: "ubiquitous" means found almost everywhere, matching more than nine out of ten homes.
Exorbitant describes a price that is far too high, and the text says nothing about cost.

questions.p: Egypt's 1919 revolution was ______ by the British authorities' arrest and exile of the nationalist leader Saad Zaghloul and several of his colleagues in March of that year: within days of the arrests, strikes and demonstrations had spread across the country.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.e: Protests spread "within days of the arrests," so the arrests triggered, or "precipitated," the revolution. "Averted" and "mitigated" suggest the arrests reduced the unrest, which reverses the text.
ce: Averted means prevented, but the revolution happened right after the arrests.
Correct: the arrests triggered the revolution, as the protests within days show.
Nothing was hidden; the arrests caused visible, nationwide protests.
Mitigated means made less severe, but the protests grew quickly after the arrests.

questions.p: Many animals that live in caves have, over many generations, lost their eyes. The Mexican tetra gives biologists an unusual opportunity to study this change. The species includes both eyed fish that live in rivers and blind fish that live in nearby caves, and the two forms can still interbreed. By crossing them and examining the offspring, researchers can identify which genes are involved in the loss of eyes.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To explain why one fish species is especially useful for studying how cave animals lose their eyes
To argue that cave fish lost their eyes more quickly than other cave animals
To describe how blind cave fish find food without using their eyes
To compare the river and cave habitats where the Mexican tetra lives
questions.e: The text presents the Mexican tetra as an "unusual opportunity" and explains why: its two interbreeding forms reveal the genes behind eye loss. The "habitats" choice takes a minor detail as the purpose.
ce: Correct: the text shows how eyed and blind forms that can interbreed let researchers find the genes involved.
The text makes no comparison of speed with other animals.
Feeding is never discussed.
Habitats are mentioned only to identify the two forms, not compared.

questions.p:
The following text is from an original story written in the style of a nineteenth-century novel. Miss Pemberton has just arrived to teach at a village school.
The schoolroom was smaller than she had imagined, and colder. Two of the windowpanes had been replaced with brown paper, and the stove in the corner gave off more smoke than heat. __Yet on every desk, Miss Pemberton noticed, a slate had been wiped perfectly clean and a pencil laid beside it, as if in readiness for a guest of honor.__ She drew off her gloves and resolved that she would not, after all, write to her sister that evening to complain.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It shows that the village could easily afford new supplies for the school.
It explains why the schoolroom was colder than Miss Pemberton had expected.
It introduces a detail suggesting the pupils' care and eagerness that contrasts with the poor condition of the room.
It reveals that Miss Pemberton had taught in this schoolroom before.
questions.e: After describing the cold, shabby room, the underlined sentence ("Yet…") shows desks prepared with care, a hopeful detail that leads to her decision not to complain. It does not explain the cold, which comes from the windows and stove.
ce: Paper windowpanes and a smoky stove suggest the opposite.
The cold is explained by the paper windows and weak stove, not by the slates.
Correct: "Yet" turns from the shabby room to the carefully prepared desks, which change Miss Pemberton's mood.
She "has just arrived" and had only imagined the room.

questions.p:
Text 1
In the mid-twentieth century, many architects argued that public housing should follow standard designs created by experts. Repeating a single well-planned apartment layout across thousands of units, they claimed, would give every family the same light, fresh air, and modern plumbing while keeping costs low.

Text 2
Studying a housing project built in the 1950s, researcher Salma Ibrahim found that the apartments residents rated most highly were not those that best matched the original plans but those that families had altered over the years by adding rooms, moving walls, or turning balconies into kitchens. Housing works best, Ibrahim concludes, when its design leaves room for residents to adapt it to their own needs.
questions.q: Based on the texts, how would Ibrahim (Text 2) most likely respond to the architects' approach described in Text 1?
c: She would argue that a single fixed design cannot meet the varied needs of families and that housing should allow residents to change it.
She would agree that standard designs are best because they keep building costs low.
She would argue that residents care less about plumbing and fresh air than about the size of their apartments.
She would claim that the architects' designs failed to provide light and fresh air.
questions.e: Ibrahim found that homes families had changed were rated highest, so she would question a single repeated layout and favor designs that residents can adapt. The "light and air" choice invents a criticism Text 2 never makes.
ce: Correct: the homes residents changed were rated highest, so she would favor adaptable designs.
Ibrahim says nothing about costs, and her findings favor altered homes, not fixed designs.
Ibrahim never ranks plumbing, air or size.
Text 2 does not criticize the light or air; it is about adaptability.

questions.p: According to an older view of expertise, chess masters succeed mainly because they can calculate many more moves ahead than beginners can. Studies beginning in the mid-twentieth century complicated that view. When shown a board from a real game for only a few seconds, masters could reproduce the positions of the pieces far more accurately than beginners; when the pieces were placed randomly, however, the masters' advantage largely disappeared. Researchers concluded that much of masters' skill lies in recognizing familiar patterns built up over years of play.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Chess masters have a much better general memory than beginners do.
Chess masters' skill depends heavily on recognizing familiar patterns from experience, not only on calculating moves.
Chess masters calculate fewer moves ahead than beginners do.
Beginners could match chess masters if they were shown the board for longer.
questions.e: The text corrects the "calculation" view with studies showing that masters' advantage depends on meaningful positions, so the main idea is pattern recognition built from experience. The "general memory" choice is the trap the random-board result rules out.
ce: The random-board result shows their advantage is not general memory.
Correct: this is the conclusion the studies led to, correcting the older view.
The text never measures how many moves either group calculates.
The text says nothing about longer viewing times.

questions.p: Biologist Amr Shalaby hypothesizes that a species of tree frog changes its skin color mainly in response to temperature, becoming paler when it is warm, rather than in response to the color of its surroundings.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Shalaby's hypothesis?
c: Frogs kept at the same temperature became paler on light backgrounds and darker on dark backgrounds.
Frogs became paler when the temperature rose, whatever the color of their surroundings.
Frogs kept in warm, light-colored enclosures were paler than frogs kept in cool, dark enclosures.
Frogs were more active at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures.
questions.e: If frogs at one fixed temperature still changed color with their background, the background, not temperature, is driving the change, which weakens the hypothesis. The warm, light enclosure finding mixes both factors, so it cannot weaken it.
ce: Correct: with temperature held constant, color still followed the background.
This supports the hypothesis instead of weakening it.
Temperature and background change together, so this cannot show which one matters.
Activity is not skin color, so this is irrelevant.

questions.p: Historian Rana Fouad argues that the 1918 influenza pandemic was underreported in the newspapers of several countries fighting the First World War, partly because wartime governments restricted news that they feared might damage public morale.
questions.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Fouad's argument?
c: In some countries, the pandemic killed more people than the war itself did.
Newspapers in countries at war printed lists of battle casualties nearly every day.
Newspapers in Spain, which was neutral in the war and had looser press restrictions, published far more reports on the epidemic in 1918 than newspapers in countries at war did.
Doctors in countries at war wrote about the epidemic in medical journals during 1918.
questions.e: Fouad links low coverage to wartime restrictions, so evidence that a neutral country with looser restrictions reported far more supports her. The death-toll finding is striking but says nothing about why reporting was limited.
ce: This shows how serious the pandemic was, not why it was underreported.
This concerns war news, not coverage of the epidemic.
Correct: where restrictions were looser, coverage was much greater, which fits her explanation.
Medical journals are not the newspapers in question, and this says nothing about restrictions.

questions.p:
Average score on a vocabulary test, by study method and time of test
Study method | Tested after 5 minutes (%) | Tested after 1 week (%)
Rereading | 81 | 42
Practice testing | 75 | 61

Psychologist Laila Morsy compared two study methods. She found that rereading seemed more effective when students were tested right away, but that ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
c: students who reread the words scored 81% when tested after five minutes.
practice testing was more effective after one week, with an average score of 61% compared with 42% for rereading.
students who used practice testing scored 75% after five minutes and 61% after one week.
both methods led to lower scores after one week than after five minutes.
questions.e: "But" signals a reversal of the five-minute result, so the blank must show practice testing ahead after a week (61% vs 42%). The "both methods fell" choice is true but does not complete the contrast.
ce: This repeats the first half of the finding and does not complete the contrast.
Correct: it shows the advantage reversing at one week, completing the contrast.
It gives one method only, so it shows no comparison.
True, but it does not show the reversal that "but" sets up.

questions.p:
Measles vaccination and reported cases in Country Q
Year | Children vaccinated (%) | Reported cases
2000 | 55 | 8,200
2005 | 72 | 3,900
2010 | 88 | 1,100
2015 | 94 | 240

A health researcher claims that as the share of vaccinated children in Country Q rose, the number of reported measles cases fell sharply. ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researcher's claim?
c: In 2015, 94% of children in Country Q were vaccinated.
Between 2000 and 2015, the share of vaccinated children rose from 55% to 94%, while reported cases fell from 8,200 to 240.
Reported cases fell from 8,200 in 2000 to 3,900 in 2005.
In 2010, there were 1,100 reported cases and 88% of children were vaccinated.
questions.e: The claim links two trends, rising vaccination and falling cases, so the evidence must show both over time; only the 2000–2015 choice does. The 2000–2005 choice shows falling cases but leaves out vaccination.
ce: One figure for one year cannot show a change over time.
Correct: it shows both trends over the whole period.
This shows cases only, not the rise in vaccination.
A single year cannot show either trend.

questions.p: Art historian Dina Kamel examined a sixteenth-century altarpiece in which the robe of the central figure is painted in ultramarine, a blue made from lapis lazuli that was often more costly than gold, while the robes of the surrounding figures are painted in azurite, a much cheaper blue. Kamel found no sign that the ultramarine had run short: the painter applied it generously, even in the robe's deepest folds. Kamel therefore concludes that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the painter deliberately reserved ultramarine for the central figure, most likely to mark that figure's importance.
the painter could not afford enough ultramarine to use it throughout the altarpiece.
azurite was more highly valued than ultramarine in the sixteenth century.
the surrounding figures were added to the altarpiece by a later painter.
questions.e: Since ultramarine did not run short, using it only for the central figure must have been a deliberate choice to set that figure apart. The "could not afford" choice is the trap that Kamel's finding rules out.
ce: Correct: plenty of ultramarine was available, yet it was used only for one figure, so the choice was intentional.
The generous use of ultramarine shows that it did not run short, so lack of money is not the best explanation.
The text says azurite was much cheaper.
Nothing suggests a second painter; the text discusses only color choices.

questions.p: In one study, participants sitting alone in a room heard what sounded like someone falling and crying out in pain in the next room. Most of them went to help within a minute. Other participants heard the same sounds while sitting with two strangers who, following the researchers' instructions, did not react at all. In this second condition, far fewer participants went to help. These results suggest that ______
questions.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: people often cannot hear sounds from a nearby room when strangers are present.
whether a person decides to help can be shaped by how the people around them respond.
people who are alone are generally kinder than people who are in groups.
the strangers in the second condition did not want anyone to help.
questions.e: The two conditions differ only in whether calm strangers were present, and helping fell when they were, so others' reactions influence the decision to help. "Kinder" overgeneralizes from one experiment.
ce: All participants heard the same sounds; the difference was how others reacted.
Correct: the only difference was the strangers' lack of reaction, and helping dropped.
Too broad: the study measures one situation, not general kindness.
The strangers were following instructions; their wishes are never described.

questions.p: The Egyptian Feminist Union, founded in 1923 by Huda ______ campaigned for women's right to vote and for better education for girls.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "Founded in 1923 by Huda Shaarawi" is extra information that opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "campaigned." A dash does not match the opening comma.
ce: Correct: the comma closes the extra information that began after "Union".
The opening comma after "Union" needs a matching closing comma.
A semicolon would separate the subject "The Egyptian Feminist Union" from its verb "campaigned".
Mismatched pair: extra information opened with a comma cannot close with a dash.

questions.p: Some bacteria survive antibiotics without being resistant to them. These so-called persister cells simply stop growing while the drug is ______ they begin growing again, and the infection can return.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "These so-called persister cells simply stop growing while the drug is present" and "afterward, they begin growing again…" are both complete sentences, so a semicolon is needed before "afterward." A comma there creates a comma splice.
ce: Correct: a semicolon joins the two complete sentences, and a comma follows the transition "afterward".
Comma splice: "afterward" is not a conjunction, so a comma cannot join the two sentences.
Run-on: the two sentences are fused, and "afterward" seems to belong to the first sentence.
Comma splice: the sentences are still joined only by a comma.

questions.p: The Art Deco style, which flourished in the 1920s and 1930s, drew on a surprising range of ______ ancient Egyptian ornament, which became highly fashionable after the discovery of Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922; the bold geometry of Cubist painting; and the sleek lines of modern machines.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: "The Art Deco style … drew on a surprising range of sources" is a complete sentence that introduces a list, so a colon is correct. A semicolon cannot introduce a list.
ce: A semicolon must join two complete sentences, and the list that follows is not one.
With no punctuation, the list runs directly into "sources" and the sentence is confusing.
Correct: a colon after a complete sentence introduces the list of sources.
"That" makes the list into a clause with no verb, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

questions.p: In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays while experimenting with cathode-ray tubes in his laboratory in Würzburg, ______ months, doctors in several countries were using the new rays to locate broken bones.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: Both parts are complete sentences, so a semicolon is needed between them. A comma alone creates a comma splice.
ce: Comma splice: two complete sentences joined only by a comma.
Run-on, and "Würzburg, Germany within months" reads as if the discovery took months.
Correct: a semicolon joins the two complete sentences.
"That" makes the second clause ungrammatical.

questions.p: By the time the Statue of Liberty was dedicated in New York in 1886, it ______ across the Atlantic from France in hundreds of pieces packed into crates.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The shipping happened before another past event (the dedication in 1886), so the past perfect "had been shipped" is needed. "Has been shipped" links the action to now, not to 1886.
ce: Present tense does not fit an event before 1886.
Future perfect does not fit events in the 1880s.
Correct: "By the time" + a past event needs the past perfect for the earlier action.
Present perfect connects to the present, not to a point in 1886.

questions.p: The museum's two portraits by the painter Fouad Ragheb, completed in the 1930s, were restored last year; conservators removed layers of yellowed varnish from ______ surfaces.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The surfaces belong to the two portraits, a plural noun, so the plural possessive "their" is correct. "Its" is singular, and "it's" and "they're" are contractions.
ce: Correct: plural possessive referring to the two portraits.
Singular, but it refers to the two portraits.
"It's" means "it is," which makes no sense here.
"They're" means "they are," not a possessive.

questions.p: Sami Adly worked for ten years in a Cairo hospital before he took up carving full time. Trained as a physician before turning to sculpture, ______
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: Sami Adly's carved figures reflect a detailed knowledge of human anatomy.
Sami Adly brought a detailed knowledge of human anatomy to his carved figures.
a detailed knowledge of human anatomy is evident in Sami Adly's carved figures.
there is a detailed knowledge of human anatomy in Sami Adly's carved figures.
questions.e: The opening phrase describes someone trained as a physician, so the subject that follows must be Sami Adly himself. "Sami Adly's carved figures" is the tempting trap, but the subject there is the figures, not the man.
ce: Dangling modifier: the figures were not trained as a physician.
Correct: the person who was trained, Sami Adly, comes right after the modifier.
Dangling modifier: knowledge was not trained as a physician.
Dangling modifier: no person who could be "trained" follows the phrase.

questions.p: Among the treasures in the medical school's archive ______ a set of anatomical drawings made by students in the 1880s, some of them still marked with their teachers' corrections.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.e: The sentence is inverted: the subject "a set of anatomical drawings" comes after the verb, and "set" is singular, so "is" is correct. "Treasures" and "drawings" are plural nouns that tempt a plural verb.
ce: Plural verb, but the subject that comes after the verb, "a set," is singular.
Plural and a progressive form that does not fit a description of a collection.
Plural verb, so it does not agree with the singular subject "set".
Correct: in this inverted sentence the subject is "a set," which is singular.

questions.p: Many scientists of the 1890s doubted that radio waves could be sent far beyond the horizon, since the waves were thought to travel in straight lines and would therefore head off into space as the Earth curved away beneath them. ______ in December 1901, Guglielmo Marconi reported receiving a signal in Newfoundland that had been sent from Cornwall, England, more than 3,000 kilometers away.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: Experts doubted long-distance radio, yet Marconi received a signal across the Atlantic, so "Nevertheless" signals the contrast. "Consequently" wrongly presents the success as a result of the doubts.
ce: Marconi's success was not caused by the scientists' doubts.
Correct: the success came despite the experts' doubts.
The success is not similar to the doubts; it goes against them.
The second sentence does not restate the first; it contradicts it.

questions.p: Psychologists have long treated boredom as an unpleasant state to be avoided. Some recent studies suggest that it may serve a purpose. In one experiment, participants who first completed a dull task, copying numbers from a phone book, later came up with more creative uses for everyday objects than participants who skipped the dull task. ______ boredom may push the mind to search for stimulation, leading to more original ideas.
questions.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.e: The final sentence states what the experiment suggests, so a conclusion word like "Thus" fits. "For example" is wrong because the sentence moves from the specific result to a general idea, not the other way.
ce: The last sentence agrees with the experiment; nothing is conceded.
The last sentence explains the result rather than contrasting with it.
The last sentence is a general explanation, not an example of the experiment.
Correct: the last sentence draws a conclusion from the experiment.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Helen Keller (1880–1968) was an American author and activist.
• An illness left her deaf and blind before she was two years old.
• Her teacher, Anne Sullivan, taught her to communicate by spelling words into her hand.
• In 1904, Keller graduated from Radcliffe College.
• She was the first deafblind person to earn a bachelor's degree.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize Keller's achievement in spite of a challenge she faced. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Anne Sullivan taught Helen Keller to communicate by spelling words into her hand.
Although an illness left her deaf and blind before she was two, Helen Keller graduated from Radcliffe College in 1904, becoming the first deafblind person to earn a bachelor's degree.
Helen Keller, an American author and activist, lived from 1880 to 1968.
In 1904, Helen Keller graduated from Radcliffe College.
questions.e: The goal needs both a challenge and an achievement, and only one choice links them (deaf and blind from infancy → first deafblind graduate). The "graduated in 1904" choice gives the achievement without the challenge.
ce: This focuses on the teacher's method, not on Keller's achievement.
Correct: it states the challenge and the achievement together.
This gives basic facts but no challenge or achievement.
This gives the achievement but not the challenge that makes it remarkable.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Cheetahs are wild cats found mainly in Africa.
• Greyhounds are a breed of domestic dog.
• Cheetahs can reach about 100 kilometers per hour.
• Greyhounds can reach about 70 kilometers per hour.
• Both animals have a flexible spine that bends and stretches with each stride, lengthening the stride and helping them run fast.
questions.q: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between cheetahs and greyhounds. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Cheetahs and greyhounds both run with a flexible spine that bends and stretches with each stride, lengthening the stride and helping them reach high speeds.
Cheetahs are wild cats found mainly in Africa, while greyhounds are a breed of domestic dog.
Cheetahs can reach about 100 kilometers per hour, much faster than the roughly 70 kilometers per hour that greyhounds can reach.
Greyhounds can reach about 70 kilometers per hour.
questions.e: Only one choice describes something the two animals have in common, their flexible spine. The speed comparison mentions both animals but uses them to show a difference.
ce: Correct: it states a feature the two animals share.
This stresses a difference, not a similarity.
This compares speeds to show a difference.
This gives one fact about one animal only.

questions.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Impressionism was an art movement that began in France in the 1860s and 1870s.
• In 1874, a group of artists including Claude Monet held an independent exhibition in Paris.
• One of Monet's paintings in the exhibition was titled Impression, Sunrise.
• A critic mocked the painting in a review and called the artists "Impressionists."
• The artists later adopted the name themselves.
questions.q: The student wants to explain how the Impressionist movement got its name. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Impressionism was an art movement that began in France in the 1860s and 1870s.
In 1874, Claude Monet and other artists held an independent exhibition in Paris.
The name "Impressionism" came from a critic who mocked Claude Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, shown at an independent exhibition in Paris in 1874; the artists later adopted the name themselves.
questions.e: To explain the name, the sentence must link the painting's title, the critic's mocking term and the artists' adoption, which only one choice does. The "Impression, Sunrise" choice names the source but not how the name arose.
ce: This dates the movement but does not explain its name.
This sets the scene but never mentions the name.
This gives the painting's title but not how it led to the movement's name.
Correct: it traces the name from the painting's title to the critic's mockery to the artists' adoption.

blocks.title: After the test
items: **Read the reason for every choice**, including the questions you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason, not by luck.

**List your weak skills.** Use your score by skill and write down every skill where you lost two or more questions, plus the trap that caught you (reversed, too extreme, half-right, off-topic, nearest-noun, comma splice…). The "Study these again" links take you straight to the lessons.

**Reading skills:** Words in Context and High-Value Vocabulary for SAT Reading and Writing; Text Structure and Purpose; Cross-Text Connections; Central Ideas and Details; Command of Evidence: Textual; Command of Evidence: Quantitative; Inferences.

**Grammar skills:** Sentence Boundaries; Extra Information: Commas, Dashes and Brackets in Pairs; Semicolons: Joining Two Complete Sentences; Colons: After a Complete Sentence; Subject–Verb Agreement; Pronoun–Antecedent Agreement, Clarity and Consistency; Verb Tense and Aspect; Verb Finiteness: Gerunds, Participles and Infinitives; Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers; Plurals and Possessives. **Writing skills:** Transitions; Rhetorical Synthesis (Student Notes).

**Redo every question you missed** after the lesson and its practice page, without looking at the reasons, and say aloud why each wrong choice is wrong. Then take Practice Test 7 under the same timed conditions.
